<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - Project Type: An open-source Swift package (KeyboardKit) that provides a customizable keyboard engine & utilities for building iOS keyboard extensions with SwiftUI.  
   - Purpose: Supply a core framework of keyboard features (actions, layouts, autocomplete, emojis, feedback, etc.), integration points for host apps & keyboard extensions, plus a Demo app illustrating usage and two keyboard targets (standard & Pro).  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   Top-level grouping:  
     • .github & scripts: CI, build, packaging, versioning pipelines  
     • Sources/KeyboardKit: the core framework organized by feature domains (Actions, Autocomplete, Callouts, Dictation, Emojis, Feedback, Gestures, Input, Layout, Localization, Navigation, Previews, Proxy, Resources, Status, Styling)  
     • Sources/_Dependencies & _Deprecated: bundled third-party code and legacy code paths  
     • Demo: Xcode workspace with a host iOS DemoApp, two keyboard extension targets (Keyboard, KeyboardPro), assets, settings bundles, controllers & SwiftUI views  
     • Tests: unit & UI tests for each core module, demo app tests  
     • Docs & README: documentation, Getting-Started guide  
     • Package.swift: SPM manifest  

3. Extract additional insights from README  
   - Core framework is built via SPM  
   - Demo folder showcases how to wire up a KeyboardApp → KeyboardInputViewController → SwiftUI KeyboardView  
   - Pro features (license-gated) extend core modules (autocomplete AI, localized layouts, themes)  
   - External system integrations: UIInputViewController, UITextDocumentProxy, AVAudio/Haptics, Speech (Dictation), App Groups, deep links  

4. Main components to include in the system-design diagram  
   a. Core KeyboardKit Framework  
      • Feature modules (Actions, Layout, Callouts, Autocomplete, Emojis, Feedback, Gestures, Dictation, Proxy, Styling, Status, Navigation, Localization, Previews)  
      • Public APIs: KeyboardApp, KeyboardInputViewController, KeyboardView, services & state objects, extension points (protocols & delegates)  
   b. Demo Host App (“DemoApp”)  
      • KeyboardAppView wrapper, Settings UI, deep-link handler  
      • Shares App Group with its keyboard extensions  
   c. Keyboard Extension Targets  
      • Keyboard (free)  
      • KeyboardPro (license-gated)  
      • Each has a KeyboardViewController subclass of KeyboardInputViewController, overrides setup(for:) and viewWillSetupKeyboardView()  
   d. External Services & System APIs  
      • UITextDocumentProxy (text insertion/deletion, context reading)  
      • AVAudioEngine & CoreHaptics (feedback)  
      • Speech framework (dictation)  
      • App Group UserDefaults (settings sync)  
      • File system & Bundle resources (assets, localization files)  
   e. CI/CD & Packaging  
      • .github/workflows (build, docc)  
      • scripts (build.sh, test.sh, package_framework.sh, package_docc.sh)  

5. Relationships and interactions  
   - Host App (DemoApp) <→ App Group ↔ Extensions: sync settings & license info  
   - KeyboardAppView (SwiftUI) → invokes core framework initialization  
   - KeyboardInputViewController (extension) consumes services & state from core framework  
   - Services (AutocompleteService, FeedbackService, DictationService, LayoutService, Proxy) ↔ External system APIs  
   - Feature modules communicate via the shared state object and service protocols  
   - Demo UI ↔ framework APIs for styling, theming, callouts, gestures, etc.  

6. Architectural patterns & design principles  
   - Modular feature-based architecture: each feature lives in its own submodule  
   - Dependency injection via service protocols (e.g., AutocompleteService, FeedbackService)  
   - SwiftUI + UIViewController bridging for keyboard UI  
   - License gating (Pro features enabled only when licenseKey is provided)  
   - Test-first design: extensive unit tests per module in Tests/KeyboardKitTests  
   - SPM-based distribution with bundled documentation (DocC)  

7. Guidelines for tailoring your diagram (Open-Source Library / Tool)  
   - Emphasize core vs. optional (Pro) modules  
   - Show extension points (protocol-driven services) and where consumers can inject custom implementations  
   - Highlight how the DemoApp initializes and configures the keyboard extension  
   - Illustrate the flow: Host App → KeyboardApp → setup(for:) → services & state injection → KeyboardView rendering → user input → UITextDocumentProxy → autocorrect/callouts/feedback  

8. Diagramming best practices  
   - Use distinct colors/shapes for:  
       • Core framework modules (grouped boxes)  
       • Optional Pro modules (dashed or different tint)  
       • Host App and Extension targets (separate sections)  
       • External System APIs (cloud icons or external boxes)  
   - Label each component clearly (module name, target name)  
   - Draw directional arrows to show:  
       • Data flow (e.g., user tap → GestureHandler → ActionDispatcher → UITextDocumentProxy)  
       • Dependency flow (e.g., KeyboardInputViewController depends on AutocompleteService protocol)  
   - Annotate key extension points (e.g., “Override viewWillSetupKeyboardView() to supply custom KeyboardView”)  
   - Optionally number major steps in the runtime initialization path  

By following these steps, you’ll produce a comprehensive, accurate architecture diagram that highlights KeyboardKit’s modular design, its integration with iOS keyboard extension APIs, and the demo components that illustrate real-world usage.  
</explanation>
